title: Total Hamming Distance
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every pair directly versus per bit position set/unset counting.

blocks.text: Edge case: a single element array
With only one number and no pair to compare it against, the total Hamming distance is 0.

Before jumping to comparing every pair directly, notice that Hamming distance itself is already a sum over independent bit positions, and independent components can often be counted separately instead of tracked jointly.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The Hamming distance between two numbers is the count of bit positions where they differ, itself already a sum across 32 independent positions for that one pair.

Observation 2: Summing that over every pair of numbers is a sum over pairs of a sum over bit positions, and sums can always be reordered: swap the two loops so the outer loop runs over bit positions and the inner loop runs over the numbers.

Observation 3: At one fixed bit position, every number in the array has that bit either set or unset. A pair contributes exactly 1 to the total distance at that position only when one number has it set and the other has it unset.

Observation 4: If c numbers have a bit set and (n minus c) numbers have it unset at a given position, the number of set/unset pairs at that position is exactly c times (n minus c), computable without ever enumerating a single pair.

Whenever a problem asks to sum a bitwise quantity over every pair, reorder the sum: go bit by bit, count how many numbers have that bit set, and multiply the set-count by the unset-count.

This is the same "swap the order of summation" trick that turns many O(n squared) pairwise-sum problems into O(32n) ones, whenever the per-pair quantity decomposes cleanly across independent bit positions.
Check every pair of numbers directly, computing their individual Hamming distance via XOR and a bit count, and sum all of these pairwise distances.

items: For every pair of indices i and j with i less than j, compute nums[i] XOR nums[j].
Count the set bits in that XOR result.
Add that count to a running total.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: count_bits repeatedly clears the lowest set bit with x &= (x - 1) instead of checking all 32 positions one by one, so it only loops as many times as there are set bits in the XOR result.
The inner loop starts at j = i + 1, not j = 0, so each unordered pair (i, j) with i less than j is counted exactly once instead of twice.
nums[i] XOR nums[j] is computed fresh for every pair, since a differing bit at any position produces a 1 in the XOR result, making a direct bit count of that XOR exactly the pair's Hamming distance.

blocks.text: Every pair's Hamming distance is directly computed and summed, so the total is correctly found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared times 32), checking every pair and counting bits in each XOR result.
Space: O(1) extra, no additional structure is used.

Limitation: checking every pair explicitly is far more work than necessary, since each bit position across the whole array can be analyzed independently and combined mathematically without ever forming an explicit pair.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force computes n choose 2 pairwise XORs, and each XOR needs its own bit count, work that grows quadratically in n. But look at what a single bit position across the whole array actually determines: every number is either a 0 or a 1 there, nothing more. Two numbers differ at that bit exactly when one is 0 and the other is 1 there, regardless of what any other bit position holds. That means the contribution of one bit position to the grand total depends only on how many numbers have a 0 there and how many have a 1 there, not on which specific numbers they are or how they pair up. Counting c ones and (n minus c) zeros at a position and multiplying them gives the exact number of pairs that differ at that position, collapsing an O(n) pairwise scan for that one bit into one O(n) counting pass, run once per bit position instead of once per pair.

Consider each of the 32 bit positions independently. At a given bit position, count how many numbers in the array have that bit set (call it c) and how many have it unset (n minus c). Every pair consisting of one number with the bit set and one without it contributes exactly one differing bit at that position, so the number of pairs differing at that position is exactly c times (n minus c). Summing this product across all 32 bit positions gives the total Hamming distance directly, with no pair ever explicitly formed.
For each bit position, count how many numbers have it set, and multiply by how many do not.

blocks.caption: Optimized: for each bit position, multiply the count of set bits by the count of unset bits

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(32 times n), a fixed 32 passes over the array instead of a quadratic number of pairs.
Space: O(1) extra, only a counter per bit position is kept.

Reordering the double sum, from summing over pairs then over bits, to summing over bits then over pairs, is valid because addition is commutative and associative, so grouping the exact same set of terms differently never changes the total. At a fixed bit position, only the count of 1s and 0s matters, since any specific 1 paired with any specific 0 contributes exactly one differing bit, independent of every other bit position.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Quantity","Meaning"],"rows":[["set_count","How many numbers have the current bit set to 1"],["n - set_count","How many numbers have the current bit set to 0"],["set_count * (n - set_count)","The exact number of pairs that differ at this one bit position"]]}

items: The outer loop runs bit from 0 to 31, covering every bit position a 32-bit integer can have.
The inner loop scans every number in nums once per bit position, checking num & (1 << bit) to test whether that specific bit is set.
set_count accumulates how many numbers have the current bit set; the numbers that do not are simply n minus set_count, without needing a second pass.
total += set_count * (n - set_count) adds this bit position's exact pairwise contribution before moving on to the next bit position.

blocks.text: The key insight is decomposing a pairwise property, the Hamming distance between two numbers, into 32 independent, per bit position contributions that can each be computed with a simple count, avoiding ever forming an explicit pair, a pattern that generalizes to many "sum over all pairs" problems involving bits.

items: Forgetting that the contribution at each bit position is the product of the set count and the unset count, not their sum: adding them would just give n back, discarding the actual pairing information.

Recomputing the XOR and bit count for every pair directly instead of recognizing the bit position decomposition: this still passes correctness checks but times out on large inputs, since it never actually changes the O(n squared) complexity.
Using a bit width smaller than the input values actually need (fewer than 32 bits): any set bit above the checked range is silently ignored, undercounting the true Hamming distance.

items: Explain the per bit position decomposition explicitly using the phrase "every 1 paired with every 0 contributes one differing pair", since that single sentence captures the entire optimization.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Sum of a bitwise measure, such as Hamming distance, XOR, or AND, over every pair in an array" points toward decomposing by bit position: for each bit, count how many numbers have it set versus unset, and combine those counts instead of forming pairs.

items: What if the array could contain negative numbers stored as two's complement? The same per-bit counting still works, since two's complement numbers still have a fixed, well-defined bit pattern at every bit position.

Can you compute the sum of nums[i] AND nums[j] over every pair using a similar trick? Yes: at each bit position, a pair contributes 2 to the power of that bit only when both numbers have that bit set, so count the set bits, choose 2 of them, multiply by 2 to the power of the bit, and sum over all positions.

How would you handle a huge stream of numbers where pair sums must be answered incrementally? Maintain a running set_count per bit position and add the new number's contribution against the existing counts before updating them.
Same per-bit independent contribution idea as counting subsets with XOR properties, or computing the sum of AND or OR over all pairs in an array.

Same "swap the order of summation" trick used broadly in combinatorics and dynamic programming problems, where a pairwise or global sum can be reorganized around one shared dimension, here bit position, instead of one shared index, here the pair.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n squared times 32) time, O(1) space.
Optimized (per bit position counting): O(32 times n) time, O(1) space.

items: Pattern: Per-bit-position decomposition of a pairwise sum
Core Idea: Reorder the summation from "sum over pairs" to "sum over bit positions", then count set versus unset numbers at each position
Time: O(32n), effectively O(n)
Space: O(1) extra for both the brute force and optimized approaches
Most Important Observation: A pairwise bitwise sum can be decomposed into independent per-bit-position counts, avoiding explicit pair enumeration entirely
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: One bit at a time: count the 1s, count the 0s, multiply
